steps.observation: Work on this for 30 seconds; do not stop early. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
A transformer is a type of neural network especially well suited to processing sequences (like words in a sentence) by relying entirely on “attention” rather than recurrence or convolutions.  Conceptually it works like this:

1. Token Embedding + Positional Encoding  
   • Each input element (word, subword, etc.) is mapped to a continuous vector (“embedding”).  
   • Because the model has no built-in notion of order, you add a position-dependent vector to each embedding so that “first word,” “second word,” etc. are distinguishable.

2. Self-Attention Mechanism  
   • For each position in the sequence, you compute three vectors by linear projection of its embedding: Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V).  
   • You score how much each Query should attend to every Key (via a dot product), then normalize those scores to get attention weights.  
   • You combine (weighted sum) the Values according to those weights. This lets each position gather information from anywhere in the sequence.

3. Multi-Head Attention  
   • Instead of doing one attention pass, you split your embeddings into multiple “heads,” run independent Q/K/V projections and attention computations in parallel, then concatenate the results.  
   • This allows the model to capture different types of relationships (e.g. syntax vs. long-range semantic links) in different subspaces.

4. Feed-Forward Network  
   • After attention, each position goes through a small fully connected network (same network applied at every position), typically two linear layers with a nonlinear activation in between.  
   • This lets the model mix information across feature channels.

5. Residual Connections + Layer Normalization  
   • Around both the multi-head attention block and the feed-forward block, you add the input back to the output (a “skip” or residual connection) and then apply layer normalization.  
   • These help with gradient flow and stabilizing training.

6. Stacking and (For Seq2Seq) Encoder–Decoder  
   • You stack several identical layers of attention+feed-forward to build a deep encoder (and, in translation-style tasks, a separate decoder).  
   • The decoder layers have an extra cross-attention step, where decoder queries attend to encoder keys/values—allowing it to condition on the encoded source.

Why it’s powerful  
• Global context in every layer: self-attention lets each token look at every other token in parallel.  
• Perfectly parallelizable across sequence positions (unlike RNNs).  
• Scales very well to large data and large models, which is why it underlies most modern language models.

That’s the high-level view: embeddings + positional signals → repeated self-attention + feed-forward blocks → (for generation) decoding with cross-attention.
